hero.name: Tenzin
hero.who: a 26-year-old trekking guide in Manali who drifts through his days and fears the future

story.b: Every winter, when the high passes close, Tenzin has four free months in Manali. Each year he plans to use them to start his own trekking company. Get the permits, make a simple website, improve his English. Instead the days dissolve. He wakes late, plays carrom at a café in Old Manali, scrolls, and helps his mother at her momo stall when she asks. He has bought three business books and read the first chapter of each. Every spring he says next winter. Now his friend Dorje, who runs a homestay, wants to partner with him on treks. Tenzin wants to say yes. But a cold fear sits in his stomach about losing his savings.

ask.q: Tenzin wastes each off-season and fears the big step. What does he need most right now?
o: More business books, so he feels fully ready before deciding
To wait for a winter when he feels calm and confident
To start living deliberately now, beginning with how he spends his days
ask.why: Waiting for confidence has already cost him several winters, and more books only add to the pile he never finishes. Time is the one thing truly his, and it is slipping past. Looking honestly at how his days go is the first step to using them well.

chapters.take: Someday is where good plans go to wait forever.

story.b: Tenzin buys a small notebook from a stationery shop on Mall Road and writes down how he spends every hour for one week. The result shocks him. Two hours a day on his phone. Three hours of carrom. Almost an hour arguing in the drivers' group about tourist rates. Not a single hour on the trek business he talks about all the time. He does not punish himself. He just makes a few choices. Mornings, nine to twelve, now belong to the business: permit forms, route notes, a list of gear. Carrom moves to after five. He mutes the drivers' group. By the end of the second week, the permit file is finally done.

ask.q: His friends call Tenzin for a long carrom session at ten in the morning. What should he do?
o: Say he will join at five, after his morning work on the business
Join them, since off-season mornings do not really count
Quit carrom and those friends completely to save every hour
ask.why: Treating mornings as if they do not count is exactly how his winters vanished. Cutting off friends entirely goes too far and will not last. Guarding his best hours for what matters, and keeping fun for later, lets him take his time back without losing joy.

chapters.take: Notice where your hours go, then take back the ones that matter.

story.b: The three half-read business books sit on Tenzin's shelf like a silent complaint. A friend sends him a list of ten more. Tenzin is tempted, then stops. He picks the plainest of the three, a guide to running a small tour business, and starts again from page one. Each morning he reads one chapter slowly, with a cup of butter tea, and copies one useful thought onto a card. Work out every cost before you set a price. Ask every guest one question at the end of a trip. He tries each thought the same day. When he finishes the book, he reads it a second time and finds things he missed. The other two books can wait.

ask.q: A friend sends Tenzin a list of ten great business books. What should he do with it?
o: Download all ten and skim each one for the main points
Finish the one good book he has, then choose one more
Read the first chapter of each to see which grabs him
ask.why: Skimming many books feels like learning, but little sticks, and first chapters are exactly where he always stops. Staying with one good book and carrying one thought into each day lets the ideas actually shape his work.

chapters.take: One book truly absorbed beats ten books half read.

story.h: Three days of rice and dal
story.b: Tenzin's fear has a shape. If the business fails, he will lose his savings and have to live simply for a year. So he decides to try that life on purpose, for just three days. He eats plain rice, dal and thukpa at home, skips the café and its pastries, walks instead of taking his bike, and wears his oldest jacket. On the first day it feels like punishment. On the second he notices he is warm, fed and laughing with his mother. On the third he walks to Vashisht and back and enjoys every step. He remembers he grew up with less than this and was happy. The lean year he feared suddenly looks survivable.

ask.q: Tenzin still fears a lean first year. Which practice fits the idea best?
o: Avoid thinking about money problems, so the fear does not grow
Live very simply for a few days, to see that it is survivable
Save for five more years before even considering the partnership
ask.why: Avoiding the fear lets it stay vague and huge. Saving for five more years is just another way of waiting. A few days of plain food and simple living show him, in his own life, that losing comfort is not the end, and the fear loosens its grip.

chapters.take: Try a little hardship on purpose, and the fear of it shrinks.

story.b: Tenzin notices that his evenings happen at two tables. At one, the café gang laugh whenever he mentions permits. They call him a big businessman, and he ends up mocking his own plans to fit in. At the other sit Dorje and Pema didi, an older guide who has run her own treks for years. They ask him about routes and costs and share their own mistakes. He always leaves Pema didi's table with a list of things to do. So he chooses. Three evenings a week now go to Dorje and Pema didi, planning over tea. He still waves to the café gang and plays a game on Sundays. But he stops sharing his dreams where they get laughed at.

ask.q: The café gang laugh whenever Tenzin talks about his trek plans. What should he do?
o: Stop sharing his plans with anyone, so nobody can laugh at them
Keep spending most evenings there, to prove them wrong
Spend more time with people who lift him, and stay friendly with the rest
ask.why: The people around him slowly shape his habits and hopes. Hiding his plans from everyone also cuts him off from those who could help, and staying with the mocking crowd to prove a point keeps him in their drag. Choosing company that lifts him, while staying kind to old friends, protects his growth.

chapters.take: Spend your time with people who make you better.

story.b: The partnership papers are ready, and Tenzin must put one and a half lakh rupees into tents and stoves. The night before signing, the dread returns, heavier than ever. He cannot sleep. Instead of scrolling, he switches on the lamp and writes the fear down plainly. What exactly am I afraid of? Losing the money. People saying I failed. Then he writes the realistic worst case. If it fails, he goes back to guiding for other companies next season, which he already knows how to do, and slowly saves again. Seen on paper, the monster is the size of one bad year. He also thinks how short a life is to spend waiting. He sleeps, and signs in the morning.

ask.q: Dread fills Tenzin the night before signing. What is the most useful thing he can do?
o: Write down exactly what he fears and its realistic worst outcome
Postpone the signing until the dread fades on its own
Scroll his phone until he is tired enough to sleep
ask.why: Dread grows when the fear stays unnamed. Postponing teaches him that fear decides, and scrolling only hides it until morning. Writing the fear and its realistic worst case usually reveals something smaller and survivable, which lets him act calmly.

chapters.take: Look straight at a fear, and it is usually smaller than the dread.

story.b: When the snow on the passes begins to melt, the first booking arrives. Four college friends from Delhi want a five-day trek with Tenzin and Dorje. Tenzin checks the gear list in the morning hours he now guards, with a cup of butter tea. He still plays carrom, but at five. The plain business book is full of his notes, and he has started a second one, slowly. Pema didi helped him with the forest permits. When one group cancels in April, the old fear rises. He writes it down, sees its real size, and calls the next enquiry. His mother notices he wakes earlier now, and hums while he packs the stoves.

chapters.take: Guard your time, keep good company, and face your fears plainly.
